title: Constrained weak identification of Allen--Cahn free energies with surface-tension calibration
abstract: Phase-field trajectories governed by the Allen--Cahn equation determine the effective force $G=F'/\eps^2$, but not the free-energy potential $F$ and interfacial scale $\eps$ separately. We introduce surface-tension-calibrated Allen--Cahn identification (STAC), a two-step method that resolves this ambiguity using an independently supplied surface tension. First, space--time weak moments produce a linear inverse problem without differentiating the measured field. A Bernstein representation with positive coefficients enforces two stable pure phases and a single central energy maximum. Second, the surface tension fixes the remaining scale algebraically. We prove scale equivalence of the forward model, uniqueness of the calibrated pair within this class, and finite perturbation bounds that remain valid when the potential vanishes at the pure phases. Experiments with resolved synthetic phase fields separate the effects of the structural constraint, ridge regularization, and constitutive approximation error. Across 80 shared noisy records, unconstrained degree-five regression produces six potentials with an incorrect well structure. Positivity combined with ridge regularization eliminates these violations and reduces the mean force error from 8.70\% to 5.66\%. Lower-degree models are nevertheless more accurate in some tests, and an admissible law outside the positive Bernstein family shows how the constraint can introduce approximation bias. STAC thus recovers a structurally admissible, physically scaled potential while making explicit which information comes from the observed dynamics and which comes from the independent surface-tension datum.
summary: This paper addresses the ambiguity in determining the free-energy potential and length scale from phase-field dynamics governed by the Allen-Cahn equation. It introduces the STAC method, which uses an external surface-tension measurement to resolve this ambiguity. The technique proves robust by combining weak-form analysis with structural constraints, leading to accurate physical parameter recovery.
main_problem: The core challenge is the ill-posed inverse problem of recovering the underlying free-energy potential ($F$) and interfacial scale ($\varepsilon$) from phase-field observations governed by the Allen-Cahn equation.
main_result: The proposed STAC method successfully recovers a structurally admissible and physically scaled potential by combining weak moment analysis with an independent surface-tension calibration, significantly improving accuracy over unconstrained methods.
method: STAC is a two-step process: first, solving a linear inverse problem using space-time weak moments and enforcing structure via a Bernstein representation; second, algebraically fixing the scale using an independently supplied surface tension ($\sigma$).
model_or_system: The system is described by phase-field trajectories governed by the Allen-Cahn equation, whose energy functional involves the free energy $F(u)$ and an interfacial scale $\varepsilon$. The dynamics are analyzed via weak formulations.
key_observables: Effective force ($G = F'/\varepsilon^2$), surface tension ($\sigma$), and the phase field $u(x,t)$.
important_parameters: The surface tension ($\sigma$) acts as the crucial independent calibration datum that resolves the inherent scale ambiguity in the dynamics.
main_assumptions: The method assumes the existence of a surface tension datum ($\sigma$) and relies on enforcing structural constraints (like positivity via Bernstein polynomials) to stabilize the ill-posed inverse problem.
figures_summary: The notes mention comparing error metrics (e.g., mean force error reduction from 8.70% to 5.66%) and showing structural violations in unconstrained vs. constrained methods.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the scale ambiguity of the Allen-Cahn model, introduces the STAC two-step method (weak moments $	o$ Bernstein constraint $	o$ $\sigma$ calibration), proves theoretical uniqueness, and validates the approach using extensive numerical experiments on noisy data.
why_interesting: While focused on classical phase transitions, the mathematical framework of solving ill-posed inverse problems using structural constraints (like positivity or specific functional forms) is highly relevant to identifying unknown Hamiltonians or effective potentials in complex quantum many-body systems.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Approximation limit of the nonnegative cone for the admissible law Gc of Eq. (10). Left: Bernstein degree two; right: degree five. Solid line: Gc; dashed line: its best approximation with nonnegative Bernstein coefficients in L2(−1, 1). The panel titles give the relative L2 force error of that approximation (the approximation floor); the unconstrained space of each degree represents Gc exactly. No trajectory data are involved.

Figure 2: Sixth-degree-law observations on the separate 2562 dataset: circular, nonconvex, and inclusion geometries at the initial time, identification endpoint, and final time. Colors show u on a common scale and black contours mark u = 0. Contours use the cell-centred coordinates of the fields. These are the neural- comparison observations, not the 962 four-law principal ensemble.

Figure 3: Paired changes in mean force error at degree five on the principal records, in percentage points. Negative values favor the first-named method. Di- amonds indicate means over ten seed clusters, dots show the individual cluster means, and bars show nominal 95% percentile bootstrap intervals. The final com- parison uses fixed degree-two STAC as the reference.

Figure 4: Degree-five recovery of the exponential law from circular observations at noise 0.03. The unconstrained estimate (dashed) and STAC (blue) use the same moments; black is the reference. Panels (a,b) show the force and an enlargement near the origin. Panels (c,d) show the primitive and its local change from u = 0. The additional force zeros and central local minimum identify an unintended metastable mixed state.

Figure 5: Supplementary clean-data tests. (a) Exponential-force recovery and best nonnegative approximation against Bernstein degree. (b) Condition number of the weak Gram matrix in the earlier normal-equation implementation used for these records. (c) Sixth-degree-law recovery under spatial refinement with a common initial field and 24 or 48 CNAB2 substeps. These calculations are separate from the principal QR/SVD comparisons.
